cards.title_en: Byblos (Jbeil) Maritime Harbor & Cedar Trade
cards.explanation: For thousands of years, sailors in Byblos traded strong cedar timber from Mount Lebanon for papyrus scrolls from Egypt, turning their stone harbor into a busy meeting place.

cards.title_en: Myth of Isis, Osiris, and the Sacred Tree of Byblos
cards.explanation: In an ancient myth linking Egypt and Lebanon, a carved chest drifted to the shore of Byblos and became part of a great palace pillar of scented wood.

cards.title_en: Afqa Spring, Nahr Ibrahim, and the Seasonal Myth of Adonis
cards.explanation: At Afqa Cave in Mount Lebanon, melting snow carries red iron-rich earth into Nahr Ibrahim. Long ago, storytellers imagined this seasonal change as a myth of spring returning.

cards.title_en: Sarcophagus of King Ahiram & the 22-Letter Phoenician Abjad
cards.explanation: Instead of hundreds of complicated symbols, Byblos scribes used 22 sound-letters carved on stone chests like King Ahiram’s sarcophagus so sailors could write messages anywhere.

cards.title_en: Writing, Recipes, and Oral Memory as a Portable Archive in the Lebanese Diaspora
cards.explanation: When families travel far from Lebanon, they carry their favorite words, stories, and za’atar flatbread recipes like a treasure chest of home.

cards.title_en: Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) & Abbasid Translation Tradition
cards.explanation: At Baghdad’s House of Wisdom, translators worked together to turn books from Greek, Syriac, Persian, and Sanskrit into Arabic so everyone could learn from them.

cards.title_en: Scholars of Baghdad: Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Kindi, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Thabit ibn Qurra & Banu Musa
cards.explanation: Scholars like al-Khwarizmi studied numbers and stars, Hunayn translated medical books, and the Banu Musa brothers designed clever water-powered machines.

cards.title_en: Contested Chronicles: Weight-in-Gold Payments & 1258 River-of-Ink Accounts
cards.explanation: Old stories say translators were paid the weight of their books in gold—showing how much Baghdad’s people treasured learning, even if the story was exaggerated!

cards.title_en: Al-Mutanabbi Street, Shabandar Café & the International Book Solidarity Archive
cards.explanation: On Al-Mutanabbi Street, neighbors gather every week to browse books, sip cardamom tea, and share poems from all of Iraq’s communities.

cards.title_en: Cardamom Date Kleicha, Shanasheel Courtyards & Plural Diaspora Memory
cards.explanation: Help Bibi Amal stamp patterns onto date-filled kleicha cookies and repair the carved wooden shanasheel balcony that shades the courtyard.

cards.title_en: Egyptian Fanous Lanterns & Competing Fatimid/Coptic Origin Narratives
cards.explanation: How did Cairo’s fanous tradition begin? Some stories tell of a starry welcome parade over a thousand years ago, while others point to old streetlamps that lit up the city at night.

cards.title_en: Cairo Lantern Metalwork, Stained Glass & Khayamiya Tentmaker Appliqué
cards.explanation: Cairo artisans fit coloured glass into brass frames to make fanous lanterns and stitch geometric flower patterns onto khayamiya cloth.

cards.title_en: Neighborhood Soundscapes: The Musaharati Drummer & Festive Cairo Chants
cards.explanation: In Cairo neighborhoods, the musaharati taps a small drum and greets families by name while children swing glowing lanterns.

cards.title_en: Teta Samira’s Koshari & Inclusive Courtyard Hospitality
cards.explanation: Layer fluffy rice, lentils, pasta, tangy tomato sauce, and crispy onions in order to serve warm bowls of Egyptian koshari to the neighbors.

cards.title_en: Egyptian Diaspora Celebrations & Ontario Egyptian Heritage Month Candidate Fact
cards.explanation: In diaspora neighborhoods, Egyptian families host heritage days where friends fold paper fanous lanterns and learn Arabic words together.

cards.title_en: The Traboules of Vieux Lyon and La Croix-Rousse
cards.explanation: In Lyon, covered walkways called traboules let neighbors walk right through stone courtyards and down hill stairs without getting caught in the rain.

cards.title_en: The Canuts of La Croix-Rousse & Jacquard Punch-Card Silk Weaving
cards.explanation: Silk weavers in Lyon called canuts used cards with punched holes to guide their tall looms, creating bright patterns and carrying the silk through covered passages.

cards.title_en: Cour des Voraces, Labor Mutualism & Historical Memory in Lyon
cards.explanation: The Cour des Voraces is a famous Lyon courtyard with a giant outdoor stone staircase where silk workers met to support their neighbors.

cards.title_en: The Mères Lyonnaises & Eugénie Brazier: Women-Led Culinary Craft
cards.explanation: The Mères Lyonnaises were famous women cooks in Lyon—like Eugénie Brazier—who opened their own welcoming restaurants and taught apprentices their craft.

cards.title_en: Galette des Rois, Kitchen Brigade Teamwork & Transnational Pastry Exchange
cards.explanation: Organize the kitchen team to bake a golden galette des rois and compare it with ma’amoul cookies while checking that every guest has a safe, allergy-friendly slice.

cards.title_en: Bibimbap (Goldongban) & Regional Variants: Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong & Andong
cards.explanation: Across Korea, different towns make bibimbap in their own way: Jeonju uses yellow mung-bean jelly and bean sprouts, Tongyeong adds ocean greens, and Andong seasons with mild soy sauce.

cards.title_en: Competing Origin Narratives of Bibimbap: Ritual, Court, Agriculture & Lunar New Year
cards.explanation: Why did people start mixing rice and vegetables together? Some stories point to busy harvest picnics in the fields, while others point to New Year’s Eve family dinners.

cards.title_en: Obangsaek (오방색): Five-Color Cultural Symbolism & Harmony of the Bowl
cards.explanation: Korean cooks and artists use five traditional colours called Obangsaek—green/blue, red, yellow, white, and black—to make every bowl and hanbok look balanced and bright.

cards.title_en: Jeonju Hanok Village, Giwa Roofs, Nambu Market & Pungnammun Gate
cards.explanation: In Jeonju Hanok Village, hundreds of wooden homes with curved giwa roofs and paper screens stand near the busy Nambu Market and Pungnammun Gate.

cards.title_en: Shared Bowls, Chuseok Songpyeon & Korean Diaspora Cultural Continuity
cards.explanation: Whether in Jeonju or far away, families steam half-moon songpyeon over pine needles and share colourful bowls around the table to celebrate together.
